utterances.text: How long would you say that you were outside in the facility that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: What do you mean? Could you please clarify it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. It was perhaps not a good question. You were able to be outside the office. How much of that day did you spend outside the office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Only as long as we needed to do whatever we needed to do, that is, go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to ask you now, please, about the period after the 19th of May, between then and your release. As far as Goran Jelisic is concerned, I suggest to you, Witness K, that you did not hear him at any time between the 19th of May and the end of May at the camp or see him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 19th of May, when we talked to that military person, at that moment, I did not hear his voice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Mr. Greaves, could you rephrase your question, please? I have the feeling that you did not really ask a question there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You've told us that after the 19th of May, you thought you heard Jelisic yelling from outside the camp, having been prevented from coming in. The question is this: Are you possibly mistaken about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I put it to you that you are, in fact, wrong, because he was elsewhere and not at all in Brcko in that period, between the 19th of May and the end of May.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: You know what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have stunned us several times. We're not trying to confront the two answers. This is a traditional institution. You ask questions. What you think about the questions you can say during your closing arguments, but this is a form of intimidation, I can tell you this right now. You have the right to think whatever you like but prove what you say. This is the last time I'm going to tell you this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I asked that question because my learned friend, earlier today, made the observation that he wanted a specific issue put to a witness so that the witness could deal with it. That is what I have done because he's asked that that should be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not making questions here. Ask a question. That's your role. Your role is to ask questions and it is the role of the witness to answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness K, I'd like --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And if we could now please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How did the doctor die, (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Dr. (redacted) was brought together with me the first night. He was terribly beaten. Those were not bruises; those were haematomas. I know health work, and I know what it means when your blood vessels are injured. So he had very serious haematomas. He was trampled by their feet. He was beaten up with a baton. He was battered severely in the camp. I heard about his brother, that his brother really invested great effort and plenty of money to have him released. Perhaps somebody else was helping him. He spent some time in the camp with us for a while, and then they took him away, I don't know where, but he was separated from us. I don't know after how many days he was released, but I heard from my fellow workers that he was simply -- after a while, his heart broke, quite simply. He suffered from severe depression, and he was trying to contain the pain, just as I was trying to do. Whether he was simply weaker than I was, was it simply that he could not stand any more all that was happening to us and that nobody reacted to that, that nobody from the outside world reacted to it --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm going to cut you off because we don't need to go into these matters in the greatest detail. But this is the doctor who was crying when you returned or you saw women returning from the sexual assaults you've told us about? Is this the same man; yes or no? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: He died after the events and in the circumstances that you've told us about. Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: After the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. You were asked about bodies that you saw on the street. At a later stage, did you ever see bodies by the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. As we were taken to clean the houses of those lords and masters, to work for their ladies, because there were a lot of rubble and splintered glass and all that, and we went to clean that up so they could live there. It just happened that we were returning sometime in the afternoon, when the visibility was still good, and somewhere at the level of the bridge, there was a slight elevation and you could see the Sava River. I just happened to cast a look at the river, and I saw bodies floating in the river --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Forgive my interrupting you. Was that before or after the change in regime that was brought about on the 19th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So that before the 19th of May, you were being taken from time to time to Brcko to clean the houses of the Serbs or their wives; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And one day you saw these bodies. Roughly how many bodies did you see in the river, if you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Three or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: -- can remember? If you can't remember, please don't guess.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Three or four, because it was just a glance. I cast a look, I saw them, I got frightened, and I diverted my eyes so that the driver wouldn't notice that I had been looking in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You were asked about the incident where you say that you saw a number of men standing against the wall and you heard an instruction given to prepare the ammunition and then to fire, and you were asked whether you were wrong about saying you saw anyone fall to the ground or not. Just tell me this: Did you hear one gunshot or more than one gunshot after the instruction to fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: More than one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is that many more or just one or two?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: More -- not one or two. More than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked whether, as a result of what had happened to you at the beginning of your detention in Luka, you weren't able to take in the details of what was going on. Were you able to take in the details of what was going on, Witness K?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you just clarify this point? What do you mean by "what was going on" or when I was moving about?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think it was being suggested to you or asked of you whether or that, by reason of what had happened in the very first place, you simply couldn't remember and you couldn't take in the various things that were being done in your presence. So you were really being asked, "Well, is your memory entirely unreliable?" That's what was being raised with you, and I want you to tell the Judges whether you were able to take in what you saw and whether what you told the Judges is the truth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You've been asked about your identification of the man called "Adolf." Remind the Judges: How much of his name did you learn at Luka? Was it just his first name or was it both of his names that you learned at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: He introduced himself as Goran Jelisic; in other words, he said to us that he represented the "Serb Adolf," the "Adolf" of the Serb people, and that it was his duty to cleanse the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'll ask you to repeat that. So he gave you the name "Goran Jelisic." In your time was there one or more than one man using the name "Goran Jelisic" or using the name "Adolf"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You've been asked about a description of a young man, blonde, up to 30 years old, with blue eyes, and an icy look. The rest of the description that you gave of this man, which was summarised, is as follows: "He was the most fearful man I ever saw. He has no conscience. He is the king of fear. He was the manager of the camp, the boss, and he pushed other perpetrators to be more fearful." Then you went on to give the description that you've been asked questions about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the admissibility of this question. Part of the cross-examination was about the physical description only of the man. The issue went to the issue of identity, not as to his personal characteristics in terms of behaviour, and in my submission, it is improper for these questions to be put.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I resist that completely. It's wholly appropriate for a complete passage of identifying to be identified for the witness. It was only identified in part. What I read out is the passage referred to in its proper context. The question I desire to ask is related to that passage and to the identification of the person she there identifies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The objection is overruled because you yourself, Mr. Greaves, you are calling into question the witness's ability to make identifications. It's true that you decided to ask questions on physical aspects such as the colour of the eyes, which are somewhat more complex to describe within the context where the witness was, but this is a point which deals with other identifying possibilities of Goran Jelisic by the witness. You can ask your question, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The description of yours that I've read out, who was the man you were there describing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Goran Jelisic, the "Serb Adolf," as he had called himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You were asked specific questions about your ability to recognise that man or to point him out. When you came into this courtroom a couple of days ago, were you then in a position to recognise the man or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How long --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How long did it take you, from the moment that the court convened, to recognise the man Goran Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not even a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Will you please now point him out to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: I like to wish his sight. I am waiting seven years for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you have any doubts about that being the man who was in the room when the beatings were going on, that being the man who introduced himself as Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have no other re-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Nice. Let me now turn to Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Witness K. I'm sorry not to call you with your lady's name, just a letter, so that nobody would recognise you. I'm trying to understand a little bit more some of your statements. You mentioned that Jelisic declared that he was the man responsible for everything happening. I'll try to quote it exactly: "That he was the man in charge and nothing can be done without his permission." Now, that was his declaration, but on the ground what were the facts? Did the facts corroborate this declaration or was it just somebody boasting about his power and, in fact, it was not so strong?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that this was not boasting at all. That was my own perception as well, and I tried to remain capable of perception. He enjoyed killing. He enjoyed showing his force, showing that he was God; in other words, that he was our judge, that he decided on our fate, and that he had all the strength and all the responsibility for everything that was going on in that camp, and that he was in charge of everything that was going on in that camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So in other words, the other people who were committing atrocities were acting according to his will? Nobody was acting independently or having a different policy of torture or of killing or that sort of thing; it was all under his auspices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Also among the declarations that you mentioned of Jelisic when he introduced himself as the "Serb Adolf," he announced that he wanted to stop any proliferation of Muslims, and these are almost your words: "And cleanse the room for the Serbs," which means -- now, "Cleanse the room for the Serbs" --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: -- could be through extermination; killing, some of the killings you mentioned; and, of course, there are other methods. There could be deportation, carrying them out to other places where they can join what is happening in some parts of the world. So was deportation also included or was it only extermination?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Extermination. He even pointed out, in connection with extermination, that Serbs could have ten houses apiece, that they could expand, that it was their territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, my last question is concerning what happened when this high officer came and you presented a complaint about the bad treatment and he promised there would be a change, and, in fact, there was a change; there was better treatment. Nevertheless, you mentioned that Jelisic came and tried to dash into the rooms to finish you up, and he called you vipers, if I remember. Is this, according to your understanding --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: -- that this kind of policy was not an execution of a general policy but it was Jelisic's policy himself? This extermination was his own policy, even if his superiors didn't want it? That was almost the impression we had.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: You know what? I had very brief contact with this gentleman in uniform. He gave us a guarantee, and that guarantee was maintained. I do not know what Jelisic did afterwards. I had only one contact after that, when he dashed into our room and when he wanted to kill us. I cannot claim what he did; I can only say for sure exactly what he said, and he acted in accordance with what he had said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What he said at that moment when he came in or before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Before. Before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So he did not even take into consideration what this high officer promised you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: As he was trying to get in to kill us, he expressed the wish to kill, to exterminate us, he said. He said that if he ever saw us anywhere, that we were his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What do you call "us"? Who are "us," women or all the people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: "Us," the persons who were in that room. Us women; we who had made this objection to the military man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Rodrigues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Witness K.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two questions to ask you. My first is that we know that Mr. Jelisic did not participate, nor was he present during the sexual assaults. My question is to know whether Mr. Jelisic knew that these rapes were being perpetrated, if you have any information which would allow you to conclude that Mr. Jelisic knew this was going on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Since he had pointed out that he was in charge and that he had to know about everything that was going on in the camp, I believe that he did know what was going on in the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My other question, Witness K, is this: If today Mr. Jelisic, among other things, because of the colour of his hair, if today he had blonde hair, would it be possible for you to recognise him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness K.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness K, I have no specific questions to ask you. You have been here for many days now in order to be subjected again to these hearings, to tell us everything you told us, to speak about your great sufferings. One thing I wanted to say before you went back home is during these hearings, did you have the feeling that you were able to say everything that you wanted to say? Were you able, through the questions that you were asked by the Judges, the Prosecution, by the Defence, did you have the feeling that you were able to express yourself as you thought you would be able to when you came before this International Tribunal? If not, if you have anything you wish to add, do not hesitate to do so now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to say that I felt a great duty as a person who worked in the field of health for so many years, as I helped people, that it came as a shock to me to encounter such persons. I could not have imagined that such people existed. It was a profound feeling of conscience that compelled me to come to this court to express my own pain and the pain of the other people who suffered and who were killed in such a brutal way. It is on my conscience to convey their pain and suffering too. We had quite a few things that we shared, and that is why I came to convey this; although, it seems to me that I could not have conveyed everything. I perhaps did not convey the depth of this pain, the intensity of this pain, but I did, to the best of my ability. I was afraid. I also had stage fright here, but I feel this profound grief for those people who were killed in such a brutal way and who were mistreated in such a way. I would also like to send a message to the Judges and to the entire world that I hope that this genocide does not happen to anyone ever again and that it is a terrible thing that could happen to any people. I am not a racist. I do not distinguish between people according to the colour of their skin or religion. I can only distinguish between people in terms of whether they are criminals or whether they commit good deeds. I tried to muster the strength to come here for seven years, to face justice and to face crime. I want that crime to be condemned, to condemn it to the extent as grave as it was, nothing more, nothing less. I want it to be well balanced. I want the condemnation to be equal to the crime committed. I want to say that I am not blaming Goran Jelisic. He has made himself guilty through the things he did. I came here to tell the truth, and I want the souls of the people who were killed to rest in peace. I want my soul to be at peace. Perhaps Goran Jelisic's conscience will awaken and he will think about all the things that he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We thank you. You have shown a great deal of courage, and, of course, we hope that you leave here more peaceful than you did when you arrived in this judicial institution. After that, in their souls and in their conscience, the Judges will come to the decision as to the exact responsibility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One more thing. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We wish you Godspeed back to your beautiful country and hope that you will find serenity and peace there. Thank you. Please do not move. You're still under protective measures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we can adjourn the session, and we will resume on Monday at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: at 1.24 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 13th day of September, 1999, at 2 p.m.
